clue.text: Churchill, perhaps, managed to achieve record height

blocks.note: ran is to have managed, as one runs a business
to do something is to achieve it
an LP is a long-playing record
H is the standard abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: Winston Churchill is credited with a record-breaking climb to some great height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Churchill' suggests Winston, but the definition is any Churchill: Randolph was both Winston's father and his son.
explanation.definitionFit: Randolph is a forename borne by two famous Churchills, so it is an example of a Churchill, flagged by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Be sure about subscriber

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
a subscriber to a club or society is a member

explanation.surface: Make certain about a person who pays a subscription.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works as in 'remember to lock up', meaning be sure to.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'remember to do it' is the same instruction as 'be sure to do it', so the phrases are interchangeable.

clue.text: Rover with leg cocked, barking

indicators.note: a cocked leg is lifted up, and in a down clue going up means reading backwards

blocks.note: on, the leg side in cricket
barking (mad) is British slang for crazy

explanation.surface: A dog called Rover lifts its leg and barks.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side. 'Rover' looks like a dog's name but means a wanderer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rover is someone who roams from place to place, just as a nomad wanders without a fixed home.

clue.text: Fashioned on one club, one I am in very rarely

indicators.note: something fashioned is shaped or made into a new form, so the letters are reworked

blocks.clueFragment: on one club, one I am
blocks.note: taken letter for letter, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone describes a fashionable club they belong to but seldom visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One I am in' sounds like club membership; only 'in' is a link, the rest is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom refers to the rare second full moon in a month, so it means extremely seldom.

clue.text: Paper featuring roguish chaps in part

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the word that follows

blocks.note: first letter of PT, the abbreviation for part, which wraps round the rest
arch means mischievous or roguish
chaps are men
end of PT, closing round the rest

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about some roguish fellows in a minor role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roguish' looks like an anagram signal, but it is simply ARCH, as in an arch smile.
explanation.definitionFit: Parchment is a writing material made from animal skin, and also a stiff paper imitating it.

clue.text: A goddess daughter entertained

blocks.note: taken as written
a Muse is one of the nine Greek goddesses of the arts
D is the abbreviation for daughter in genealogies

explanation.surface: A goddess's daughter played host to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertained' reads as hosted guests, but it means kept amused.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been entertained has been diverted and made to smile, i.e. amused, a past participle in both.

clue.text: Pays Emerald Isle criminal - I won't say a word

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so the letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A crook pays off Ireland and promises total silence.
explanation.walkthrough: The Emerald Isle is Ireland; here it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a promise to keep a secret, which is saying one won't say a word.

clue.text: Boy has two notes for docker

blocks.note: a boy's name
do and re, the first two notes of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A lad is given a couple of banknotes as a tip for a dock worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' suggests money but means musical notes of the do-re-mi scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A stevedore is a worker who loads and unloads ships, a synonym for a dock labourer.

clue.text: Hate Department of Employment evaluation

blocks.note: DE was the abbreviation of the former UK Department of Employment
a test is an evaluation

explanation.surface: Someone loathes being assessed by the employment office.
explanation.walkthrough: The Department of Employment was a UK government ministry, abbreviated DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to loathe intensely, a strong synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Hurt? One must ring hospital

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so it goes inside

blocks.note: an ace is a one in cards
H is the map symbol for hospital

explanation.surface: Injured? Someone must phone the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like phoning but means surround.
explanation.definitionFit: To hurt, as in 'my leg hurts', is to ache or give pain, the same intransitive verb.

clue.text: Take off La Bohème character beginning to corpse

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: Mimì is the consumptive heroine of Puccini's opera
first letter of corpse

explanation.surface: An opera performer's character begins to corpse, theatre slang for breaking into giggles on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: To corpse is actors' slang for laughing helplessly mid-scene; here it just supplies its first letter. 'Take off' means imitate, not remove.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to parody or impersonate them, which is exactly what a mimic does as a verb.

clue.text: Look back on extremely rare harvest

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of rare
to harvest is to gather in or collect

explanation.surface: A farmer reminisces about an exceptionally unusual harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely rare' reads as 'very rare', but it asks for the ends of rare.
explanation.definitionFit: To recollect is to remember, to look back on past events in one's mind.

clue.text: Film show after the witching hour

indicators.note: after places the word before it at the end, behind the following item

blocks.note: the witching hour is traditionally midnight
to show feelings is to express them

explanation.surface: A cinema screening that begins after midnight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film show' looks like one phrase, but it splits: Film is the definition, show is wordplay. Midnight Express is Alan Parker's 1978 prison drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Midnight Express is a 1978 movie about an American jailed in Turkey, so it is a film title.

clue.text: Willingly accept loving hug

blocks.note: first meaning: to welcome an idea or change eagerly
second meaning: an affectionate holding in the arms

explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense and the noun sense are simply set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works both as a verb for eagerly adopting something and as a noun for an affectionate clasp in the arms.

clue.text: Surgeon confined to bed developed a reaction to a burn?

definitions.text: developed a reaction to a burn?

indicators.note: someone confined to a place is kept inside it

blocks.note: Joseph Lister, the British surgeon who pioneered antiseptic surgery
taken as written

explanation.surface: A surgeon laid up in bed has had a bad reaction to a burn.
explanation.walkthrough: Lister is the famous Victorian surgeon behind antiseptics. The question mark flags that the definition describes rather than defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin that blisters forms fluid-filled bubbles after a burn, so blistered describes reacting that way.

clue.text: I held back nothing from state

indicators.note: going back means the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
held means had, as in possessed
zero, nothing, looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they kept nothing back from the authorities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held back nothing' reads as being frank, but back applies only to held. 'State' means a US state, not a government.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the north-west.

clue.text: Poorly girl ringing round over blood group after one doctor confused situation

indicators.note: something poorly is in bad shape, so the letters are put out of order
ringing means circling, so something sits inside
after says the preceding material follows the next piece in the answer

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree
the letters of girl rearranged
a round shape is the letter O
O is a blood group

explanation.surface: A sick girl is circled by a doctor checking her blood group, and things get muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged girl wraps round O; in a down clue 'over' puts that above the blood group O, and all of it comes after one doctor. 'Over' here is positional only.
explanation.definitionFit: An imbroglio is an embarrassingly tangled situation, a messy predicament, from Italian for entanglement.

clue.text: Great beat, for example

blocks.note: surface reading: a superb rhythm in music
setter's reading: two words spelt alike at the end that look as though they should rhyme but are said differently

explanation.walkthrough: Great and beat end in -eat, yet one says 'grate' and the other 'beet', so they rhyme only on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye rhyme is a pair of words whose spelling matches but whose pronunciation does not, like great and beat.

clue.text: Sound home to rent

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
to let a property is to rent it out

explanation.surface: A sound home available for renting, as an estate agent might advertise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective (solid) but is a geographical noun: a sound is a narrow stretch of sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound is a channel or arm of the sea, and an inlet is a narrow arm of water running inland.

clue.text: Close to refrigerator, large jug brought in by beer maker

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept
what is brought in by something ends up inside it

blocks.note: first part of by, which wraps round the rest
last letter of refrigerator
a ewer is a large wide-mouthed pitcher
end part of by, closing round the rest

explanation.surface: A big jug kept near the fridge is delivered by a beer company.
explanation.walkthrough: The word by is both part of the indicator and the outer container, split around R and EWER.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewery is a company or plant that makes beer, so a beer maker describes it.

clue.text: Record American throwing event

blocks.note: a disc is a record
US, the United States, stands for American

explanation.surface: An American sets a record in an athletics throw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' looks like a sporting best, but it is a vinyl record.
explanation.definitionFit: The discus is a field athletics event in which a heavy disc is thrown for distance.

clue.text: Then I exercised, completely naked

indicators.note: something exercised is worked over and moved about, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
altogether means completely or entirely

explanation.surface: Someone recalls working out in the nude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercised' looks like a workout but signals rearranging. In the altogether is a jocular British idiom for nude.
explanation.definitionFit: In the altogether is an informal idiom for wearing no clothes, i.e. nude.

clue.text: Collapse, perhaps, in a Staffordshire town?

blocks.note: to collapse is to keel over; the over is implied, and turns keel round

explanation.surface: Something has fallen down in a Midlands market town.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no printed signal for turning round: collapse is keel over, and 'over' itself does the job, which is what the question mark owns up to.
explanation.definitionFit: Leek is a market town in the Staffordshire Moorlands, in the English Midlands.

clue.text: Wading bird appearing in other one

indicators.note: something appearing in a phrase is found within its letters

blocks.note: the letters running across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A wading bird turns up in someone else's patch.
explanation.definitionFit: The heron is a long-legged bird that stands in shallow water to fish, the classic wader.

clue.text: NCO bringing in last of intake for physical

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter alone
bringing something in means taking it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a corporal is a non-commissioned officer
last letter of intake

explanation.surface: A non-commissioned officer brings the last of a new intake of recruits in for a medical examination.
explanation.walkthrough: NCO means non-commissioned officer, such as a sergeant or corporal. 'Physical' looks like a noun (a medical check) but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporeal means of the body rather than the spirit, which is a synonym of physical.

clue.text: Vehicle coming from Ayr rolled over

indicators.note: letters coming from a phrase are found inside it, running across the word gap
rolled over means turned upside down, so read in a down clue's opposite direction here backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters yr-rol inside these two words

explanation.surface: A vehicle from the Scottish town of Ayr has overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayr is a Scottish coastal town. 'Rolled over' sounds like an accident, but only over is the signal; rolled is part of the source letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry is the British word for a large goods truck, a kind of road vehicle.

clue.text: Carol I had introduced - short track

indicators.note: something introduced is put into another, so it ends up inside

blocks.note: to carol is to sing joyfully
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Carol says she introduced a short song on an album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name, but it is the verb meaning sing. 'Short track' is not a brief recording but a stretch of railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A siding is a short length of railway line off the main route, where trains are parked.

clue.text: Concentrate on studies within church

indicators.note: within means inside, so the preceding pieces sit inside the next

blocks.note: first part of CE, the Church of England, which wraps round the rest
taken as written
dens are private studies or rooms for work
end of CE, closing round the rest

explanation.surface: An instruction to focus on one's studies while in church.
explanation.walkthrough: CE is the Church of England. 'Concentrate' looks like focus, but here means reduce in volume.
explanation.definitionFit: To concentrate a liquid is to reduce it by removing water, which is what condense means as a verb.
